lines.text: That's what Americans had in 401(k) plans as of June 2026, according to the Investment Company Institute.
lines.say: That's how much Americans had in 401(k) plans as of June twenty twenty-six, according to the Investment Company Institute.

lines.text: And it started as a few lines about executive pay that almost nobody noticed.
lines.say: And it started as a few lines about executive pay that almost nobody noticed.

lines.text: Along the way, it pushed aside the company pension and handed the job of funding retirement to you.
lines.say: Along the way, it pushed aside the company pension, and handed the job of funding retirement to you.

lines.text: So how did a footnote become the way most Americans retire, and what does it mean for your paycheck? Here's the plan.

lines.text: Chapter 1: A tiny rule from 1978.
lines.say: Chapter one: a tiny rule from nineteen seventy-eight.

lines.text: Rewind to 1978. Congress passes a big tax bill, the Revenue Act, and tucks in a new section called 401(k).
lines.say: Rewind to nineteen seventy-eight. Congress passes a big tax bill, the Revenue Act, and tucks in a new section called 401(k).

lines.text: In 1978, its job was narrow: clearing up how bonus and profit-sharing pay, mostly for executives and higher earners, could be put off and taxed later.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy-eight, its job was narrow. It cleared up how bonus and profit-sharing pay, mostly for executives and higher earners, could be put off and taxed later.

lines.text: Then, in 1980, a benefits consultant named Ted Benna read it differently.
lines.say: Then, in nineteen eighty, a benefits consultant named Ted Benna read it a different way.

lines.text: His idea: let ordinary workers put part of every paycheck in before income tax, and have the company add a match on top.
lines.say: His idea was simple. Let ordinary workers put part of every paycheck in before income tax, and have the company add a match on top.

lines.text: He designed one for his own firm, the Johnson Companies, but he needed the IRS to agree.
lines.say: He designed one for his own firm, the Johnson Companies, but he needed the I R S to agree.

lines.text: In November 1981, the IRS proposed rules that allowed pre-tax contributions straight from salary. That was the green light.
lines.say: In November nineteen eighty-one, the I R S proposed rules that allowed pre-tax contributions straight from salary. That was the green light.

lines.text: From there, employers started adding them. Almost by accident, a side door in the tax code became the main entrance.
lines.say: From there, employers started adding these plans. Almost by accident, a side door in the tax code became the main entrance.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Pension versus 401(k).
lines.say: Chapter two: pension versus 401(k).

lines.text: First, what got pushed aside. A traditional pension is officially a defined benefit plan.
lines.say: First, what got pushed aside. A traditional pension is officially called a defined benefit plan.

lines.text: The company promises a set check every month in retirement, for life, usually based on a formula.
lines.say: The company promises a set check every month in retirement, for life, usually based on a formula.

lines.text: For example, a formula might pay 1.5% of your final salary for every year you worked there.
lines.say: For example, a formula might pay one and a half percent of your final salary for every year you worked there.

lines.text: Our math: work 30 years, retire earning $60,000, and that's 45% of your pay, or $27,000 a year, for as long as you live.
lines.say: Our math: work thirty years, retire earning sixty thousand dollars, and that's forty-five percent of your pay, or twenty-seven thousand dollars a year, for as long as you live.

lines.text: The company sets that money aside, invests it, and eats the cost if markets go badly or you live to 100.
lines.say: The company sets that money aside, invests it, and eats the cost if markets go badly, or you live to a hundred.

lines.text: A 401(k) is the opposite: a defined contribution plan. The only thing defined is what goes in.
lines.say: A 401(k) is the opposite. It's a defined contribution plan, and the only thing defined is what goes in.

lines.text: What comes out depends on how much you put in, how it's invested, and what the markets do.
lines.say: What comes out depends on how much you put in, how it's invested, and what the markets do.

lines.text: Now watch what happened. In 1980, about 30.1 million private-sector workers were active in pensions. By 2020: about 12 million.
lines.say: Now watch what happened. In nineteen eighty, about thirty point one million private-sector workers were active in pension plans. By twenty twenty, it was about twelve million.

lines.text: Meanwhile, 401(k)-style plans went the other way: from about 19 million active workers in 1980 to about 85 million in 2020.
lines.say: Meanwhile, 401(k)-style plans went the other way, from about nineteen million active workers in nineteen eighty to about eighty-five million in twenty twenty.

lines.text: By 1990, they already had about 35 million, more than the roughly 26 million in pensions that year.
lines.say: By nineteen ninety, they already had about thirty-five million, more than the roughly twenty-six million in pensions that year.

lines.text: Of those 85 million in 2020, about 72 million were in 401(k) plans specifically.
lines.say: Of those eighty-five million in twenty twenty, about seventy-two million were in 401(k) plans specifically.

lines.text: One caution: the Labor Department counts workers who are eligible but not contributing as active. So it's who could save, not who does.
lines.say: One caution: the Labor Department counts workers who are eligible but not contributing as active. So it's who could save, not who does.

lines.text: Chapter 3: The great risk shift.
lines.say: Chapter three: the great risk shift.

lines.text: Here's the real change, in one sentence: the risk moved from the company to you.
lines.say: Here's the real change, in one sentence. The risk moved from the company, to you.

lines.text: Three risks moved. First, market risk: if stocks crash the year before you retire, your balance takes the hit.
lines.say: Three risks moved. First, market risk. If stocks crash the year before you retire, your balance takes the hit.

lines.text: Second, longevity risk. A pension pays until you die. A 401(k) pays until the money runs out.
lines.say: Second, longevity risk. A pension pays until you die. A 401(k) pays until the money runs out.

lines.text: Third, decision risk. Joining, saving enough, picking investments, and not cashing out early are all on you now.
lines.say: Third, decision risk. Joining, saving enough, picking investments, and not cashing out early are all on you now.

lines.text: Let's put a price on that shift. Remember the pension paying $27,000 a year?
lines.say: Let's put a price on that shift. Remember the pension paying twenty-seven thousand dollars a year?

lines.text: A common rule of thumb, the 4% rule, says you can take out about 4% of your starting balance in the first year.
lines.say: A common rule of thumb, called the four percent rule, says you can take out about four percent of your starting balance in the first year.

lines.text: Our math: $27,000 divided by 4% is $675,000. That's what you'd need saved on day one to match that pension.
lines.say: Our math: twenty-seven thousand divided by four percent is six hundred seventy-five thousand dollars. That's what you'd need saved on day one to match that pension.

lines.text: And that 4% comes from a 1994 study of past markets. It's a guideline, not a guarantee.
lines.say: And that four percent comes from a nineteen ninety-four study of past markets. It's a guideline, not a guarantee.

lines.text: Pensions also have a safety net. Private pensions are insured, up to limits, by a federal agency called the PBGC.
lines.say: Pensions also have a safety net. Private pensions are insured, up to limits, by a federal agency called the P B G C.

lines.text: A 401(k) has no backstop like that. If the investments fall, your balance falls.
lines.say: A 401(k) has no backstop like that. If the investments fall, your balance falls with them.

lines.text: Money can also leak out early. Vanguard says 6% of its 401(k) savers took a hardship withdrawal in 2025, a record high.
lines.say: Money can also leak out early. Vanguard says six percent of its 401(k) savers took a hardship withdrawal in twenty twenty-five, a record high.

lines.text: Back in 2020, that figure was just 1.7%.
lines.say: Back in twenty twenty, that figure was just one point seven percent.

lines.text: To be fair, pensions had a weak spot too. They reward staying put.
lines.say: To be fair, pensions had a weak spot too. They reward staying put.

lines.text: With our example formula, leaving after 5 years earns just 7.5% of final pay. That's our math.
lines.say: With our example formula, leaving after five years earns you just seven and a half percent of final pay. That's our math.

lines.text: A 401(k) moves with you. Your own contributions are always yours, and you can roll the account over when you switch jobs.
lines.say: A 401(k), on the other hand, moves with you. Your own contributions are always yours, and you can roll the account over when you switch jobs.

lines.text: Chapter 4: How a 401(k) works.
lines.say: Chapter four: how a 401(k) actually works.

lines.text: Here's the flow: money leaves your paycheck before income tax and lands in an account in your name.
lines.say: Here's the flow. Money leaves your paycheck before income tax, and lands in an account in your name.

lines.text: Then you pick investments from the plan's menu, or the plan picks a default for you.
lines.say: Then you pick investments from the plan's menu, or the plan picks a default for you.

lines.text: That tax break is the engine. For example, say you put in $3,000 while in the 12% federal tax bracket.
lines.say: That tax break is the engine. For example, say you put in three thousand dollars while you're in the twelve percent federal tax bracket.

lines.text: Our math: your federal income tax drops by $360, so your take-home pay falls by about $2,640, not $3,000.
lines.say: Our math: your federal income tax drops by three hundred sixty dollars, so your take-home pay falls by about two thousand six hundred forty, not three thousand.

lines.text: Payroll taxes still apply, and you pay income tax later, when you take the money out.
lines.say: Payroll taxes still apply, though, and you pay the income tax later, when you take the money out.

lines.text: Many plans also offer a Roth 401(k), which flips that: you pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free.
lines.say: Many plans also offer a Roth 401(k), which flips that around. You pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free.

lines.text: Then there's the match, the piece Benna built in from the start.
lines.say: Then there's the match, the piece Benna built in from the very start.

lines.text: Vanguard calls a 50% match on the first 6% of pay a typical design.
lines.say: Vanguard calls a fifty percent match on the first six percent of pay a typical design.

lines.text: For example, on a $50,000 salary, putting in 6%, or $3,000, brings $1,500 from the employer.
lines.say: For example, on a fifty thousand dollar salary, putting in six percent, or three thousand dollars, brings in fifteen hundred from the employer.

lines.text: Put in only 3%, and the match is $750. Our math: that's $750 a year less from the employer.
lines.say: Put in only three percent, and the match is seven hundred fifty. Our math: that's seven hundred fifty dollars a year less from the employer.

lines.text: That's why people call the match free money, though it's really part of your pay package.
lines.say: That's why people call the match free money, though really it's just part of your pay package.

lines.text: One catch: the employer's match can take years to vest, up to 6 under IRS rules.
lines.say: One catch: the employer's match can take years to vest, up to six under I R S rules.

lines.text: There are limits, too. For 2026, the IRS capped what you could put in from your own pay at $24,500.

lines.text: That year, workers 50 or older could add $8,000 more, and ages 60 to 63 could add $11,250 instead.
lines.say: That year, workers fifty or older could add eight thousand dollars more, and ages sixty to sixty-three could add eleven thousand two hundred fifty instead.

lines.text: Counting the employer's money, the 2026 cap on total contributions was $72,000.
lines.say: Counting the employer's money too, the twenty twenty-six cap on total contributions was seventy-two thousand dollars.

lines.text: The IRS updates these limits each year, so check irs.gov for the 2027 numbers.

lines.text: Chapter 5: The nudge era.
lines.say: Chapter five: the nudge era.

lines.text: For decades, the 401(k) had one big flaw: you had to sign up. And lots of people never got around to it.
lines.say: For decades, the 401(k) had one big flaw. You had to sign up, and lots of people just never got around to it.

lines.text: Then came the Pension Protection Act, signed on August 17, 2006.
lines.say: Then came the Pension Protection Act, signed on August seventeenth, two thousand six.

lines.text: It gave employers legal cover to enroll workers automatically and pick a default investment. Workers could still opt out.
lines.say: It gave employers legal cover to enroll workers automatically and pick a default investment for them. Workers could still opt out.

lines.text: It caught on. Vanguard says 61% of its plans used automatic enrollment at the end of 2025, up from 10% in 2006.
lines.say: It caught on. Vanguard says sixty-one percent of its plans used automatic enrollment at the end of twenty twenty-five, up from ten percent in two thousand six.

lines.text: And the default changes behavior. In 2025, 94% of workers joined in auto-enroll plans, versus 64% where they had to opt in.
lines.say: And the default changes behavior. In twenty twenty-five, ninety-four percent of workers joined in auto-enroll plans, versus sixty-four percent where they had to opt in.

lines.text: These are different plans, so it's not a perfect test. But the gap shows how much the default does.
lines.say: These are different plans, so it's not a perfect test. But the gap shows how much the default does.

lines.text: Then a 2022 law called SECURE 2.0 turned that nudge into a requirement for most new plans.
lines.say: Then a twenty twenty-two law called SECURE two point oh turned that nudge into a requirement for most new plans.

lines.text: Most 401(k) plans set up after December 29, 2022 must automatically enroll workers, starting with plan years in 2025.
lines.say: Most 401(k) plans set up after December twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-two must automatically enroll workers, starting with plan years in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: The default starts at 3% to 10% of pay and climbs 1 point a year to at least 10%.
lines.say: The default starts at three to ten percent of pay, and climbs one point a year to at least ten percent.

lines.text: Workers can still opt out. And businesses with 10 or fewer employees, or under 3 years old, are exempt.
lines.say: Workers can still opt out. And businesses with ten or fewer employees, or that are under three years old, are exempt.

lines.text: One more change kicks in with 2027 contributions: the Saver's Match.
lines.say: And one more change kicks in with twenty twenty-seven contributions. It's called the Saver's Match.

lines.text: For eligible lower- and moderate-income savers, the federal government adds 50 cents per dollar, on up to $2,000 a year.
lines.say: For eligible lower and moderate income savers, the federal government adds fifty cents per dollar, on up to two thousand dollars a year.

lines.text: That's up to $1,000, shrinking as income rises, with first deposits scheduled for 2028.
lines.say: That's up to a thousand dollars, shrinking as income rises, with the first deposits scheduled for twenty twenty-eight.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Scorecard and recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the scorecard, and the recap.

lines.text: So, did it work? Start with the good news: the pile keeps growing.
lines.say: So, did it work? Let's start with the good news. The pile keeps growing.

lines.text: Per ICI, 401(k)s held $8.9 trillion at the end of 2024, and $10.8 trillion by June 2026.
lines.say: Per the Investment Company Institute, 401(k)s held eight point nine trillion dollars at the end of twenty twenty-four, and ten point eight trillion by June twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Savers are trying, too. In 2025, the average Vanguard saver put in 7.6% of pay, or 12.1% with the employer's share.

lines.text: And the average Vanguard 401(k) balance hit $167,970 at the end of 2025.
lines.say: And the average Vanguard 401(k) balance hit a hundred sixty-seven thousand, nine hundred seventy dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: But averages get pulled up by a few giant accounts. The median saver, the one right in the middle, had $44,115.
lines.say: But averages get pulled up by a few giant accounts. The median saver, the one right in the middle, had forty-four thousand, one hundred fifteen dollars.

lines.text: Now the gap. In March 2026, the BLS found 72% of private-industry workers had access to a plan at work.
lines.say: Now the gap. In March twenty twenty-six, the Bureau of Labor Statistics found seventy-two percent of private-industry workers had access to a plan at work.

lines.text: But only 52% actually took part. So only about half of private-sector workers were saving in a plan at work.
lines.say: But only fifty-two percent actually took part. So only about half of private-sector workers were saving in a plan at work.

lines.text: Flip it around, and our math says about 28% had no plan at work to join at all.
lines.say: Flip it around, and our math says about twenty-eight percent had no plan at work to join at all.

lines.text: And the pension is now the rare one: 14% of private workers had access to one, versus 70% with a 401(k)-style plan.
lines.say: And the pension is now the rare one. Fourteen percent of private workers had access to one, versus seventy percent with a 401(k)-style plan.

lines.text: That's the trade-off. The system is open, portable and growing, but it only works for people inside it.
lines.say: That's the trade-off. The system is open, portable and growing, but it only works for the people inside it.

lines.text: Recap. One: the 401(k) began as a 1978 tax rule for bonuses, until Ted Benna turned it into a paycheck savings plan.
lines.say: Let's recap. One: the 401(k) began as a nineteen seventy-eight tax rule about bonuses, until Ted Benna turned it into a paycheck savings plan.

lines.text: Two: it replaced the pension for most private workers, and moved market, longevity and decision risk onto you.
lines.say: Two: it replaced the pension for most private workers, and moved market risk, longevity risk, and decision risk onto you.

lines.text: Three: the engine is the tax break plus the match, within yearly IRS limits, like $24,500 of your own pay in 2026.
lines.say: Three: the engine is the tax break plus the match, within yearly I R S limits, like twenty-four thousand five hundred dollars of your own pay in twenty twenty-six.

lines.say: Four: defaults matter. Automatic enrollment meant ninety-four percent participation, versus sixty-four percent, in Vanguard plans in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: The 401(k) didn't just change where retirement money sits. It changed who's in charge of it, and that's now each of us.

post.title: How a tiny 1978 tax rule became $10.8 trillion in 401(k)s
post.ig: A 1978 tax rule meant for bonuses now holds $10.8 trillion. How the 401(k) replaced the pension, explained.
post.tiktok: A 1978 tax rule now holds $10.8 trillion. How the 401(k) replaced the pension and moved the risk to you.
post.yt_desc:
A few lines added to the tax code in 1978 now hold about $10.8 trillion in 401(k) plans (ICI, June 2026). This video explains how it happened: Ted Benna's 1980 idea, the IRS's 1981 green light, and how 401(k)-style plans overtook company pensions, from about 19 million active workers in 1980 to about 85 million in 2020 while pensions fell from 30.1 million to 12 million. We break down the risk shift with real math (a $27,000-a-year pension versus the $675,000 a 401(k) would need), how the tax break and match work with the 2026 limits, auto-enrollment from the 2006 law to SECURE 2.0 and the Saver's Match starting with 2027 contributions, and a scorecard on balances and access.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Investment Company Institute, quarterly retirement market data (Q2 2026) and Fact Book (2025); US Department of Labor, EBSA, Private Pension Plan Bulletin Historical Tables (Sept 2025) and bulletin abstracts (2000, 2011, 2020), via EPI and EBRI; IRS IR-2025-111 / Notice 2025-67 (Nov 13, 2025); IRS vesting rules; Pension Protection Act of 2006 (Aug 17, 2006); SECURE 2.0 Act (Dec 29, 2022) and proposed regulations (Jan 10, 2025); Treasury/IRS Notice 2026-48 on the Saver's Match (Aug 2026); Vanguard, How America Saves 2026 (June 2026); BLS, Employee Benefits in the United States, March 2026 (Sept 25, 2026); CNBC (Jan 4, 2017) and ASPPA (2018) on the 401(k)'s history; Bengen, Journal of Financial Planning (Oct 1994).

News and education, not financial advice.
